六角手風琴以風箱推拉驅動自由簧發聲，按鈕通常分置兩端，不同於手風琴按鈕位於前方。: The concertina makes sound with free reeds driven by pushing and pulling a bellows, with the buttons usually set at the two ends, unlike the accordion, whose buttons are on the front. English and duet systems mostly have single-action reeds of the same pitch, so one button sounds the same note whether pushed or pulled and can play a chromatic scale; German systems mostly use double-action reeds, where one button changes pitch with the direction of the air. German instruments commonly use long-plate reeds, with several reeds to a note, and if their tuning differs slightly they produce a tremolo; the bandoneón usually tunes reeds an octave apart precisely, so there is little tremolo. Its sound depends mainly on the reed arrangement and the direction of the air, and the different systems respond to pitch very differently.
六角手風琴出現在古典音樂、愛爾蘭與英格蘭傳統音樂、南非傳統音樂、探戈與波卡音樂中: The concertina appears in classical music, Irish and English traditional music, South African traditional music, tango and polka. From the nineteenth century to the early twentieth, Salvation Army bands and concertina bands in the English-speaking world used it often; English morris dancing also uses the English and Anglo-German instruments. German emigrants took the Chemnitz and bandoneón to the United States and Argentina; the former became a polka instrument in the Midwest, the latter an important member of Argentine tango orchestras. Between the First and Second World Wars Germany also had accordion and bandoneón orchestras.
六角手風琴於十九世紀在英國與德國獨立發展：1829年查爾斯·惠斯通取得英國設計專: The concertina developed independently in Britain and Germany in the nineteenth century: Charles Wheatstone took out a British patent for his design in 1829, and Carl Uhlig introduced the German type in 1834. From the 1850s British makers developed the duet system because the German type could play melody and accompaniment; German keyboard systems included the Chemnitz, the Carlsfeld and the bandoneón, and by the end of the century some were unified. It then travelled to the United States and Argentina with Salvation Army bands and German emigrants, and survived in Irish traditional music, English morris dancing, Africa, polka and tango. It declined in the early twentieth century as the accordion was in demand and pianos were mass-produced, and recovered with the folk revival of the 1960s.
六角手風琴是自由簧氣鳴樂器，與手風琴、口琴同屬一個樂器家族，Hornbostel: The concertina is a free-reed aerophone and belongs with the accordion and the harmonica to one instrument family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.132. It is driven by an expanding and contracting bellows, and the buttons are usually at the two ends rather than mostly on the front as on the accordion; different systems have same-note or double-action reeds. Being small and portable it was once common among soldiers, sailors, cowboys and other people on the move, and it is used in classical music, in Irish, English and South African traditional music, and in tango.

演奏者以雙手持琴，按鈕通常位於琴體兩端。發聲依靠推拉風箱，使氣流通過自由簧。初學: The player holds the instrument in both hands, with the buttons usually at the two ends of the body. Sound comes from pushing and pulling the bellows so that air passes the free reeds. A beginner must first work out which system the instrument is: same-note systems give the same note on push and pull, while double-action reed systems change pitch with the direction of the bellows. The English system divides the scale alternately between the two hands, which suits fast melodies; duet systems mostly give the bass to the left hand and the treble to the right. German and Anglo-German instruments commonly have double-action reeds, so the button has to be chosen by direction.
